newsitem.title: CANADA: INSTANT VIEW - Canadian federal budget 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Canadian federal budget 1997/98.

text.p: Following is a list of reactions to Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin's fiscal 1997/98 budget, which was presented on Tuesday in parliament.

Martin predicted the 1997/98 budget deficit would be C$17 billion, or two percent of gross domestic product. Spending for the year beginning April 1 was targeted by Martin at C$105.8 billion, with C$137.8 billion in revenue.
Martin estimated the 1996/97 budget deficit would be C$19.0 billion, compared to a projected C$24.3 billion. He predicted a 1998/99 deficit of C$9.0 billion, or one percent of GDP.
FRED KETCHEN, SENIOR VICE-PRESIDENT, SCOTIAMCLEOD
"Paul Martin has been smart, he's probably been lucky. We're going to see low interest rates -- that will be of some assistance."
"So far I don't see any surprises in here at all, and I don't think that surprises anybody."
About the extended tax on banks: "Politically it meets with some degree of approval with some people."
About aid to hospital research: "Probably it may help some of the biotech industry. In the long run, you're going to have preventative medicine."
RICH WYLIE, ECONOMIST, TD SECURITIES
"I really don't think there were any surprises in this. With most of the stuff we had a pretty good idea that we were going to see it."
"They've got some minor spending increases but if you look at the total dollar value it's relatively low."
BOB BOAZ, DIRECTOR OF RESEARCH, HSBC JAMES CAPEL CANADA
"It's status quo. We're not going to see much of an impact tomorrow."
ANDREW PYLE, HEAD OF FIXED-INCOME RESEARCH, ABN AMRO BANK CANADA

"I think where he did fail was in not revising next year's deficit (target). I think there were a number of people who were looking for that revision and any calls for the balanced budget to be pushed one year ahead are not confirmed by this budget. So there's a possibility the market could take this as a negative, offshore players could take this as a negative,"
JOHN CLINKARD, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CIBC
"If you look behind Martin's numbers, it's really easy to get down to a deficit of C$12 billion for this year."
"Any sort of growth in the economy over the next year will make it easy to get a significantly stronger growth in revenues."
JOHN NICHOLSON, MANAGING DIRECTOR, SCOTIA CAPITAL MARKETS
"We view it as positive for the Canadian dollar. We think the Canadian dollar will do better. We expect the Canadian dollar to appreciate overnight as a result of the positive budget."
HANK CUNNINGHAM, DIRECTOR OF FIXED INCOME, FIRST MARATHON SECURITIES LTD
"I'm pleasantly surprised that (Martin) didn't disappoint us. All of us feared that there might be some tugs at the sleeves by some of the left-wing spenders."
"He's made some extremely conservative assumptions, we believe, with interest rates and growth that lead us to conclude he will continue to outperform his own targets."
BOB BOAZ, DIRECTOR OF RESEARCH, HSBC JAMES CAPEL CANADA

"It'll be two different reactions (on Wednesday) -- you'll see the foreign investors look at the C$19 billion deficit instead of C$24 billion and say 'This is great, they're way below what they previously estimated.'"

"What you're going to see tomorrow: a flow of funds into the Canadian dollar briefly, quite possibly the bond market, quite possibly the stock market, to push it higher. But it will be short-lived, because people will soon realize that a lot of positive views emanating from the positive federal deficit numbers have been discounted in the market. So you see a pop and then a fall-back."
JOHN CLINKARD, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CIBC
"(Martin)'s maintaining his conservative assumptions, he's not going out on a limb and he's not blowing the bank to get re-elected."
"This will probably have a positive effect on the dollar because it reinforces the fact that he (Martin) is continuing to do what he said."
ANITA LAURIA, ECONOMIST, SALOMON BROTHERS
About the numbers and forecasts in the budget: they will look "very conservative" upon closer scrutiny.
"Unless interest rates are a lot higher or growth is a lot weaker, it's going to become very clear that these targets are meant to be beaten."
((Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8100))
